articles.title: Preparing for next year’s Rosetta 2 demise
articles.subtitle: The reckoning is coming. Apple has done it before, and it’s doing it again. After macOS 27 Golden Gate, you will no longer be able to run legacy Intel apps using Rosetta 2.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The reckoning is coming. Apple has done it before, and it’s doing it again. After macOS 27 Golden Gate, you will no longer be able to run legacy Intel apps using Rosetta 2. After the 26.4 update in March, when running any affected app in macOS 26 Tahoe, you see a notification banner when you launch affected software or a background component launches that uses Intel code:

Support Ending for Intel-based Apps. This version of “[App Name Here]” will not open in a future release of macOS. Learn how to update to an Apple silicon version. [Learn More pop-up menu]

There is one carveout noted for “certain older, unmaintained games that rely on Intel-based frameworks,” so far unnamed.

With information in hand, you can plan how to deal with Intel-only apps that have been abandoned, or the developers have seemingly no interest in updating. Printer makers are, so far, the worst.

A history of looking backward

Apple has done this before—many times, in fact. I’ve argued in the past that one of Apple’s key strengths, and a key to the continuity of the Mac’s operating system, is how well it’s managed transitions across chip architectures, frameworks, and operating system changes. 1

Look at what Apple has managed:

Motorola 680×0 to PowerPC (silent emulator)

Mac OS 9.1 (or later) to Mac OS X (Classic)

PowerPC to Intel (Rosetta, original flavor)

32-bit to 64-bit code (warnings)

Intel to Apple silicon M-series chips (Rosetta 2)

At each of those milestones, Apple offered either advance warnings about a future lack of compatibility, an emulator tool, or both. Does anyone have fond memories of running QuarkXPress using Classic in Mac OS X in its early days? When it crashed, which was often, it only took down the Classic “app” and didn’t require a Mac restart.

To be fair, Apple could have continued to let older software run for as long as it was willing to devote time to maintaining emulators or compatibility layers. We could be using apps written for Motorola 68030s on our M5 Macs right now! However, it makes increasingly less sense to support the past after a reasonable transition, particularly one that stretches years and sees the company discontinuing compatible hardware.

Apple released the last Intel-based model in August 2020, introduced its first M-series computer in November 2020, and halted sales of computers with Intel inside in 2023.

As part of this shift, you receive the Intel software warning, not just the first time you launch an affected app or an Intel-based component or even Terminal-accessed binary runs, but the next time you do it after a restart. Yes, it is trying to bug you to get a newer version of your software. Golden Gate also pulls an interesting trick: When you upgrade, it removes the Rosetta emulator. You’re prompted to install it the first time you need Intel code. I guess this is an extra spur to remind you.

Because Intel-only apps will continue to work under Rosetta until you install macOS 28 Dumbarton, these reminders will continue for at least another 16 months or so. 2 Once you upgrade to macOS 28, those apps and components will simply stop working.

Pastebot’s Quick Menu.

Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.

Pastebot was already one of the Mac’s best clipboard utilities, capable of managing an extensive collection of copied text and images in multiple formats, PDFs, URLs, files, and HTML, along with metadata. The app can handle up to 1,500 clippings and features fast search, extensive customizable keyboard shortcuts, list and detail views of clipboard items, and iCloud sync between multiple Macs.

What sets Pastebot 3 apart is its addition of deep automation tools. articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: More Pokémon Pokopia DLC and update news revealed
articles.subtitle: Deep dive on Pokémon Pokopia DLC shows new features and quality-of-life additions Related Pokémon Pokopia receives the first stage of its three-part expansion pass, Bubbly Basin, this Wednesday.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Deep dive on Pokémon Pokopia DLC shows new features and quality-of-life additions

Related

Pokémon Pokopia receives the first stage of its three-part expansion pass, Bubbly Basin, this Wednesday. Fans are beyond excited to dive back into the game, especially now that they get to go below the surface and explore the depths of the ocean.

While teasers have given players a glance at what's to come, there's still plenty that remains a mystery. Japan's Famitsu got to try out the first part of the Pokémon Pokopia expansion pass during development. The magazine shared the experience in an intriguing article, providing new details about what's to come in Pokémon Pokopia update v2.0.0, as well as Bubbly Basin.

Confirmed to be added to the Pokédex in Bubbly Basin are Pokémon Diglett, Golisopod, Stunfisk, and Sharpedo. With the expansion pass, players will be able to build habitats for these creatures and befriend them. The base game allows players to have the Dive ability and go underwater, but they will not be able to register Pokémon, as they inhabit Bubbly Basin.

Besides Dive, gamers can use their other abilities underwater, and there is even an upgrade for the Surf move that will make their lives much easier while below the surface. In Bubbly Basin, players can obtain a blender, which allows them to make smoothies and power up Surf. Once upgraded, the move will receive a speed boost and allow players to destroy underwater blocks.

Image: Game Freak/Koei Tecmo/Nintendo

Image: Game Freak, Omega Force/The Pokémon Company

As some Pokémon Pokopia players might have a hard time keeping their bearings and may experience motion sickness, the game's developers have added visual indicators to address that. Players will be able to view the underwater action with a frame and an icon at the very center of the screen to help orientate them.

Another great feature that's coming Aug. 5 for free is a special container that can be placed in several towns. The loot inside can always be accessed regardless of where it was originally placed. In total. In total, it will have 140 free slots.

This way, players won't have to constantly fast-travel somewhere to find an item. It's a game-changing feature, especially for fans who have storage boxes scattered across the map or a large inventory and cannot recall where they might've left something. Plenty of content is coming to Pokémon Pokopia this week; gamers won't want to miss it whether they're purchasing Bubbly Basin or downloading the free update.

articles.title: If you want a MacBook Air, you should buy one ASAP
articles.subtitle: Macworld First it was the Mac mini. Then the Mac Studio. Now, the memory crisis is aiming to wipe out stock of yet another Mac, this one far more popular. If you’re looking to buy a MacBook Air, it might be hard to find one before the end of August.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
First it was the Mac mini. Then the Mac Studio. Now, the memory crisis is aiming to wipe out stock of yet another Mac, this one far more popular.

If you’re looking to buy a MacBook Air, it might be hard to find one before the end of August. As we saw with the Mac mini earlier this year, delivery estimates on Apple.com are beginning to show delays as Apple scrambles to get more stock.

As reported by Mark Gurman in his latest Power On newsletter, the seemingly minor delay on Apple. com—orders are currently shipping with a two-week backlog—is indicative of a much larger issue caused by memory shortages.

Gurman reports that Apple is scrambling to keep new MacBooks in stock during the back-to-school and upcoming holiday shopping seasons by sourcing RAM from China and “prominently steering customers toward the base MacBook Pro,” which starts at $1,999, several hundred dollars more than the $1,299 Air.

Upselling is a tactic Apple rarely deploys at its stores, and it could backfire. Apple has built a ton of trust with consumers over the years by largely letting buyers dictate the budget they want to spend, whether that means an iPad, iMac, or MacBook. Coupled with price hikes that are still fresh in people’s minds, steering consumers into higher-end products they don’t need could cross the line from sensible to sleazy.

Apple isn’t expected to update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor until spring 2027, though it’s unclear whether that will fix the issue. The M6 MacBook Air is expected to use the same LPDDR5X RAM as the current model, and there are no signs that the supply issues will ease before 2028. In its recent financial results conference call, Tim Cook reiterated that Apple is facing “a hundred-year flood on the memory pricing” and is “evaluating all options” to balance costs and supply.

On Monday morning, Amazon still had the 13-inch MacBook Air in stock for $1,243, about $50 less than the Apple Store, which was quoting an August 18-25 delivery window. Also reader David points out that Apple’s refurbished store has several in stock as well for $200 less than you’d pay for a new one. Apple refurbs come with a full 1-year warranty and go through a “rigorous” inspection process.

But whichever model you choose, you should probably act fast.

articles.title: Q3 results: 3D pricing, EGOT timing, and underestimating demand
articles.subtitle: I’m still the boss, kid. I’ve been covering Apple financial results and earnings calls for a very long time, dating back to my time at Macworld when Steve Jobs would occasionally parachute into earnings calls presided over by, among other people, Tim...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’ve been covering Apple financial results and earnings calls for a very long time, dating back to my time at Macworld when Steve Jobs would occasionally parachute into earnings calls presided over by, among other people, Tim Cook! This week’s earnings call was Cook’s 90th and final installment, and that’s probably the most notable thing about it.

Even the fact that it was a record third quarter isn’t that notable. It’s more notable when Apple doesn’t set a quarterly record, especially given economic changes and inflation.

Still, as always, the results and the earnings call provided a few things I thought were worth pointing out. And so, powered by my second cup of tea while I’m on a summer trip to visit family (that was a late-night flight!), here are some thoughts about financial things.

It’s not a chip shortage, it’s demand

Apple is having supply-constraint problems. Maybe you’ve noticed the lack of new Mac minis and Mac studios? The Mac is the hardest-hit product line when it comes to supply, but Cook said the iPhone has also been affected, and anticipates constraints on the iPad as well.

This isn’t the whole story, of course, but it is part of it—and a part that Apple wants to crow about. Apple is limited in how many Macs, iPhones, and iPads it can sell because they are all powered by systems-on-chips that are coming off of chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor’s most advanced production nodes. Here’s how Cook put it:

The root cause of it is not a regular supply issue. It’s a demand forecast issue, to be candid, where the iPhone and the Mac are both doing remarkably better than we thought they would do.

And we had high expectations, so it wasn’t that our expectations were low, but as you can see from iPhone’s growth being 22% and Mac’s growth at 29%… these are extraordinary numbers and the supply chain just has less flexibility in it than normal. So we’ve been pulling supply ahead, and at some point there’s a limit to that.

And so we’ve got a quarter that we’re going to be scrambling on the supply side, essentially. This isn’t a partner or supplier issue. This issue is an incredibly strong… iPhone and Mac product cycle that has really yielded a demand beyond our expectation.

The root cause of it is not a regular supply issue. It’s a demand forecast issue, to be candid, where the iPhone and the Mac are both doing remarkably better than we thought they would do.

And we had high expectations, so it wasn’t that our expectations were low, but as you can see from iPhone’s growth being 22% and Mac’s growth at 29%… these are extraordinary numbers and the supply chain just has less flexibility in it than normal. So we’ve been pulling supply ahead, and at some point there’s a limit to that.

And so we’ve got a quarter that we’re going to be scrambling on the supply side, essentially.

This isn’t a partner or supplier issue. This issue is an incredibly strong… iPhone and Mac product cycle that has really yielded a demand beyond our expectation.

You can’t argue with the strong iPhone and Mac sales figures, and Apple specifically called out the MacBook Pro and the MacBook Neo, which Cook said “has been especially popular” and suggested that the company is still struggling to make them fast enough.

It’s admirable (and sensible) that Cook isn’t pointing fingers at anyone but customers who want Apple products, but the key phrase in his statement is “the supply chain just has less flexibility in it than normal.” This is an acknowledgement that while in the past, Apple might have been able to boost chip production from its partners, today the chip industry is maxed out thanks to the wild building of chips for AI applications.

Still, I do take Cook at his word: Even in a normal world, there’s only so much TSMC could do to rapidly respond to a dramatic increase in chip orders from Apple. I’m sure Apple is kicking itself for not anticipating stronger demand, especially given how tight the whole industry has gotten.

And Cook’s suggestion that Apple is going to be “scrambling on the supply side” because the impact will “increase significantly ” (and Cook really emphasized that word! ) suggests that this may get worse before it gets better.

Oh yeah, and this isn’t just about cutting-edge SOCs. It goes for memory too. According to Cook, the price Apple pays for memory just keeps going up, and the offsetting Apple has been able to do by using existing inventory is going to be less effective as supplies run out.

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

Last month, as it continued to navigate the PR craters left by its thousands of layoffs and IDF patronage, Microsoft announced that it was bringing four original Xbox games to PC through a new Backward Compatibility for PC program. Now, it seems Microsoft has bigger PC port plans in store, expanding its backwards-facing content strategy.

According to reporting from The Verge, a leaked document sent to developers indicates that Microsoft is planning to enable developers to allow their previously-released Xbox 360 games to be purchased and played on PC. The Xbox 360 backwards compatibility will reportedly be available on "Xbox PCs," Microsoft's upcoming Project Helix, and handheld devices.

Expected to launch via a "gradual" rollout between 2027 and 2028, the service will reportedly let developers opt into allowing PC backwards compatibility for their games in their Xbox 360 release catalogue.

An eventual emergence of Xbox 360 backwards compatibility seemed likely, as users realized last month that the four OG Xbox games newly released for PC were running in an Xbox emulator that was, itself, running inside an Xbox 360 emulator. With "minimal" reverse-engineering, emulator developers were able to get Microsoft's nested emulation solution to run dumped Xbox 360 games.

The leaked document also provided details for the disc-to-digital program that previous Verge reporting said was in testing at Microsoft, which will allow owners of Xbox One and Xbox Series X game discs to obtain a digital license for the game across Xbox devices. Unfortunately, that service doesn't seem to extend to Xbox 360 discs; if I had to speculate, I'd guess it's because 360 discs likely lack the disc-level licensing tech that Xbox had originally planned to utilize with the Xbox One launch.

articles.title: One last time, this is Tim: Final transcript of Apple’s Q3 2026 earnings call
articles.subtitle: Tim Cook signals for victory! For the 90th and final time, Apple CEO Tim Cook hopped on a conference call with financial-industry analysts to detail the quarter gone by, give a peek at what’s to come, and maybe take one final victory lap.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
For the 90th and final time, Apple CEO Tim Cook hopped on a conference call with financial-industry analysts to detail the quarter gone by, give a peek at what’s to come, and maybe take one final victory lap. CFO Kevan Parekh and incoming CEO John Ternus were there, too.

This is Six Colors’s complete transcript of the call for July 30, 2026.

Tim Cook’s introduction

Thank you, Suhasini. Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for joining the call. Today, Apple is pleased to report $109.4 billion in revenue, up 16% from a year ago and a June quarter record. We were able to achieve this despite supply constraints and sequential foreign exchange headwinds.

We continue to see enormous customer enthusiasm for our most popular lineup ever, with iPhone revenue growing 22% from a year ago to reach a June quarter record. We saw so much excitement around the best Mac lineup we’ve ever had, growing a strong 29% to achieve a June quarter revenue record. Services also set a June quarter record with $30.7 billion in revenue.

We achieved June quarter revenue records in every geographic segment. We were pleased to see strength across the board with June quarter records in the U.S., Latin America, Western Europe, India, China mainland, Japan, and Southeast Asia. We also achieved June quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets and saw double-digit growth in most emerging markets.

This year’s WWDC was a wonderful showcase of our latest innovations. We were tremendously excited to unveil the all-new Siri AI, a completely reimagined version of Siri that is profoundly capable, deeply personal, and integrated seamlessly across our platforms. And we’ve been absolutely thrilled by the response who’ve been using Siri AI in the developer and public betas.

The reviews from early users have been phenomenal, and it’s been so wonderful to hear from people who are excited about the capabilities we’ve built. And it underscores our philosophy that building AI that is private and based on personal context can change how users find information and get things done with our products in a way that truly enriches their lives.

We really couldn’t be more excited about it, and we are feeling incredibly enthusiastic about the impact it’s going to have.

At WWDC we also announced new tools to help parents keep kids safe online and we were pleased by the overwhelmingly positive reaction. New child safety features like Ask to Browse and Time Allowances will help parents encourage kids to develop healthy digital habits. These new tools integrate guidance from leading clinical and child development research, including the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Our goal is to make it easier for parents to manage what their children see, who they interact with, and how and when they can use their devices. We’re looking forward to bringing these new capabilities to users this fall, in addition to amazing new updates across our operating systems.

Now let me turn to the results for the quarter, beginning with iPhone. iPhone revenue for the June quarter was $54. 3 billion, up 22% from a year ago. We achieved June quarter records in every geographic segment, and set a June quarter record for upgraders. According to IDC, we gained share globally during the quarter. As I’ve said before, this is the most powerful and most popular iPhone lineup we’ve ever had.

More people are relying on iPhone every day for AI, powered by the outstanding performance of A19 and A19 Pro. Across the lineup, iPhone continues to deliver the performance, battery life, durability, and camera capabilities that people count on every day.

Whether it’s the extraordinary camera system of iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, the remarkably thin design of iPhone Air, the balanced performance and durability of iPhone 17, or the exceptional value of iPhone 17E, there’s an iPhone for every customer.

Mac delivered its best June quarter yet, with $10. 4 billion in revenue, growing an impressive 29% from a year ago despite significant supply constraints. This revenue growth was driven by the incredible strength of our latest lineup, with MacBook Pro and the all-new MacBook Neo. According to IDC, we gained share globally.

We also set a June quarter revenue record in developed markets and an all-time record in emerging markets with particular strength in Greater China, where we had an all-time revenue record. In addition, we achieved all-time records for upgraders and customers new to Mac.

With the power of Apple Silicon, the Mac lineup delivers outstanding power-efficient performance, massive memory bandwidth, and next-level AI capabilities. Mac continues to be the ultimate AI powerhouse, excelling at high throughput, on-device inference, and creation across a broad range of AI workloads. And we’re seeing customers increasingly put those capabilities to work, from using Mac Mini as a powerful platform for agentic AI to deploying clusters of Mac Studio systems to run frontier-class models locally.

Across the lineup, customers continue to embrace the Mac family. MacBook Neo has been especially popular, with its distinct design and excellent value resonating with customers around the world, and we’re continuing to work hard to meet demand. MacBook Air, the world’s most popular laptop, continues to deliver the portability and performance customers love with M5.

articles.title: Running Simulators Inside Claude Code for Mac
articles.subtitle: Claude Code has a new simulator button. Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

One of the things tucked away in the small print of macOS 27 beta 3 is the news that you’ll need a 2TB iCloud+ subscription in order to use the new AI features for home security cameras in the Apple Home app.

While some are suggesting that we shouldn’t be too surprised by this, I do find it a somewhat disappointing move by Apple …

Apple announced significant AI-powered upgrades to the Home app at this year’s WWDC.

Intelligent Home app notifications

One of these was using Apple Intelligence to replace a whole sequence of individual security notifications with a single summary. At present, something as routine as a family member arriving home might generate a notification that they were seen in the driveway, then that the garage door was opened, then that the garage door was closed, then that they were seen at the front door, then that the front door was unlocked, and finally that it was locked.

In iOS 27, all of those individual notifications are replaced with a single one saying that the family member arrived home.

Three AI features for video footage

But the bigger improvements was an upgrade of HomeKit Secure Video from 1080p to 4K, and the use of Apple intelligence to analyze footage from home security cameras. Apple highlighted three intelligent capabilities.

With generated video descriptions, users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them. They can also search through camera clips so they can easily find what they’re looking for, like a package delivery. At the top of the Search page, the Home app elevates noteworthy clips that users may want to review, so they can quickly see important moments.

articles.title: Best Games for Mac 2026: A-list Mac games to play
articles.subtitle: Macworld For years, gaming on a Mac meant compromises: fewer releases, weaker performance, and the quiet assumption that serious players needed a Windows PC. That’s no longer entirely true.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
For years, gaming on a Mac meant compromises: fewer releases, weaker performance, and the quiet assumption that serious players needed a Windows PC. That’s no longer entirely true.

Thanks to Apple silicon, improved developer support, and a growing number of high-quality ports, there are now genuinely great games that run well on macOS. Not just indie experiments or casual time-killers, but full-scale RPGs, strategy games, and visually demanding titles that take advantage of modern Mac hardware.

This list focuses on the best Mac games you can play right now, not everything that technically runs on macOS. Every game here was chosen based on performance on Apple silicon, quality of the Mac version, and whether it’s actually worth your time and money. We’ve also excluded games that rely heavily on emulation or feel meaningfully worse than their Windows counterparts.

Mac gaming still isn’t perfect, but if you own a recent Mac, it’s better than it’s ever been. These are the games that prove it.

Best Mac Games to play in 2026

There are so many great games available to play on the Mac. Everyone has different tastes though, so we’ve tried to include something for everyone below. So whether you love RPGs, fighting games, action-adventure, first-person shooters, strategy games or puzzle, read on to find something to play.

Below you can find the best games released in 2025, plus the ones we loved and will continue to play in 2026. Updated August 2026 to add our reviews of Total War: Attila and Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition.

1. Age of Empires II – Legendary strategy game

More than 25 years after the original game first appeared on Mac, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition has finally arrived as a native macOS release thanks to Feral Interactive. While it has taken an extraordinarily long time to get here, the wait has been worthwhile. This remastered version updates one of the greatest real-time strategy (RTS) games ever made with sharper high-resolution graphics, bundled expansion content and Apple Silicon support, making it feel at home on modern Macs.

The game spans roughly a thousand years of history, from the Dark Ages through the Medieval era, allowing players to command dozens of civilizations in campaigns inspired by real historical figures such as Joan of Arc, Attila the Hun and Vlad Dracula.

The Definitive Edition includes the original game alongside three DLC expansions, dramatically increasing the amount of content with additional civilizations, maps and historical campaigns. Combined with skirmishes and replayable scenarios, there are hundreds of hours of strategy gameplay available.

Gameplay remains as compelling as ever. Players must gather resources, expand settlements, research technologies and build armies while responding to enemy attacks in real time. Although experienced strategy fans will quickly feel at home, the game also includes excellent tutorials that teach both basic mechanics and more advanced tactical concepts, making it approachable for newcomers.

The Mac version does have a few drawbacks. It only supports Apple Silicon Macs, leaving older Intel machines behind. Multiplayer is also restricted to Mac users, so there is no cross-platform play with Windows players. In addition, the interface occasionally shows its age, and the game does a poor job of explaining that the enhanced graphics pack requires a separate free download after installation.

Fortunately, these issues do little to diminish what is still one of the finest RTS games ever created. The updated visuals preserve the charm of the original while making battles look crisp on modern displays, and the sheer volume of campaigns and historical scenarios provides outstanding value for money.

For Mac owners who enjoy strategy games, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition is an easy recommendation. It successfully modernises a timeless classic without losing the gameplay that made it legendary, proving that great strategy games never go out of style.

2. Total War: Attila (PC) – Grand strategy meets conquest

Total War: Attila was originally launched for Intel Macs and PCs way back in 2015 – when the macOS was still called OS X.

Needless to say, changes to both Apple’s hardware and operating systems meant that the Mac version fell by the wayside several years ago, but Feral Interactive has now brought the game back to the Mac, providing native support for current Apple Silicon Macs, and Apple’s Metal graphics system (although it no longer runs on Intel Macs anymore, unfortunately).

Apple is struggling to keep the M5 MacBook Air in stock as rising memory and storage costs continue to disrupt the consumer electronics market. Buyers ordering directly from Apple now face delivery estimates stretching to the end of August, even after the company raised MacBook Air prices twice this year.

Apple increased the starting price from $999 to $1,099 when it introduced the M5 model in March, then raised it again to $1,299 in June. The latest model includes 512GB of storage instead of 256GB, although the higher price still reflects growing pressure from expensive memory and SSD components.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that retail sources describe the MacBook Air as “more constrained than they can ever recall.” Apple also added a subject-to-availability warning to its recent back-to-school promotion, which stands out because the company rarely highlights supply limits for products released several months earlier.

Memory shortages are limiting MacBook Air supply

The AI datacenter expansion across the United States has increased demand for high-end memory, forcing suppliers to shift production away from consumer-grade components. As a result, DDR5 RAM and SSD prices have climbed sharply, leaving companies such as Apple with fewer parts and higher manufacturing costs.

Gurman said Apple is exploring Chinese memory suppliers for devices sold in China while giving production priority to the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro.

“From what I’ve heard, the MacBook Air shortage is indeed tied to the ongoing memory crunch. Apple has been working to alleviate the issue by preparing to source memory from Chinese suppliers, at least for devices sold in that country.”

Apple is also prioritising the base M5 MacBook Pro as it prepares for an M6 refresh later this year, while the next MacBook Air update will reportedly arrive later.

The company has already warned that supply problems will affect sales during the coming quarter, and further component cost increases could lead to more Mac price changes. Amazon still lists some M5 MacBook Air models with next-day delivery and a $100 discount, although third-party availability may tighten as Apple’s direct stock remains limited.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.content:
Get ready for new quests, NPCs, and relationship milestones.

Related

If you’ve played Harvest Moon or are looking for a Stardew-like with shades of Zelda and a ‘90s-inspired, Sailor Moon aesthetic, this is it. Fields of Mistria is a $14 farming and life-simulation RPG created by the independent team at NPC Studio. It’s been in early access for two years, and now the full game is launching on Steam on Aug. 5.

Fields of Mistria ’s early access was incredibly well-received, earning an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating on Steam after more than 21,000 reviews. For the past two years, players have eagerly awaited pre-release updates that introduced secret bachelorettes, new farming systems, and the ability to progress quests and storylines, like the game’s labyrinthine mines system.

And for those two years, the Fields of Mistria subreddit has remained very active, with players showing off fan art, begging the devs for certain characters to become romanceable (we’re looking at you, Elsie and Olric), and constant speculation about what the full game would include.

This week, the wait is over. Here’s everything changing in Fields of Mistria version 1.0.

How much will Fields of Mistria 1.0 cost?

Fields of Mistria costs $13.99 on Steam. The team at NPC Studio has confirmed that this price will not go up with the 1.0 release.

What platforms is Fields of Mistria available on?

Right now, Fields of Mistria is available on PC and is Steam Deck compatible. The devs say to stay tuned about future ports to other platforms.

All the new additions coming to Fields of Mistria 1.0

More relationship time. The NPC heart level caps will increase from 8 to 10 hearts.

More relationship milestones. For romanceable characters, there will be 10-heart proposals, wedding events, and the ability to start families.

More NPCs. There are new Saturday Market vendors coming to town – specifically, Stillwell, a fortune teller slash wizard, and Zorel, a music vendor. (Tragically, neither appears to be a romance option.)

The conclusion of the Town Repair storyline. It’ll feel so good to see Mistria fully healed through its post-earthquake reconstruction saga.

More renown. In 1.0, the Renown Level – or the measure of how well the Mistria rebuild is going – will be raised to 100.

More requests. The town’s Request Board is getting a refresh, with new projects and fetch quests from your neighbors ready for you to tackle.

More rewards. There will be more items to collect and new museum sets to fill, along with new goodies for doing so.

For years, the pitch was simple: Macs don’t get viruses, or at least not the kind that matter. However, anyone who observed Mac security over the past couple of seasons already knows that line doesn’t hold up anymore. The MacPaw research group has prepared a report on MacOS threats by mid-2026. The new Moonlock threat report findings spell out just how far that old assumption has crumbled.

The report isn’t a marketing brochure. It’s a data dump from analysts who spend their days pulling apart malware samples. So, the picture it paints is blunter than most Apple-adjacent headlines you’ll see this summer. Mac and Windows, according to Moonlock, are no longer separate battlegrounds. This shift toward a shared, cross-platform threat surface means attackers are running the exact same campaigns against both systems. They just swap the binary depending on which OS shows up.

Set us as a preferred source and our Apple reporting ranks higher in your Google Search results and Discover feed — one tap, no account changes.

The Transition to Other Platforms No One Wanted

Here’s the part that should get your attention if you manage even a handful of Macs. Moonlock’s researchers found campaigns using identical servers, identical domains, and the same operators to hit MacOS and Windows users. It’s not two separate criminal groups anymore. It’s one group with two toolkits. So, it’s a big reason Mac security conversations sound so different this year compared to 2024.

This tracks with what other shops have been saying for a while. Jamf’s Threat Lab flagged similar overlap earlier this year. He pointed to a DPRK-linked operation that shipped seven distinct MacOS malware families in a single campaign. Also, it was running alongside Windows tooling the whole time. For everyday users this shows up in a less abstract way too.

General internet security threats advice built around “I’m on a Mac, so I’m fine” is over. Mac threat prevention now needs to be treated with the same seriousness IT teams have long applied to Windows fleets.

ClickFix Still Wins

If you’ve spent any time in Mac forums or security Twitter this year, you’ve run into the term ClickFix. It’s not flashy. There’s no zero-click exploit, no kernel-level trickery. It’s just a fake CAPTCHA or a bogus “fix this error” popup. It walks a user through pasting a command into Terminal themselves. Also, it’s the backbone of most current ClickFix social engineering attacks.

That’s the whole trick, and according to Moonlock it remains the single most common way attackers get onto a Mac. Microsoft’s own Digital Defense Report clocked ClickFix at roughly 47% of observed initial access across 2025. That momentum carried straight into 2026. Instead of standard identity verification pages, lures are increasingly being used.

These are disguised as artificial intelligence tools, borrowing the appearance of popular chatbots and programming assistants. Their goal is to trick people into lowering their guard against basic Mac security practices.

Odyssey Stealer Is Having a Moment

If ClickFix is the delivery method, Odyssey is often what’s riding inside. articles.content:
Anthropic just launched a brand-new desktop app called Claude Science. The new app joins the main Claude app on the Mac, which includes Claude AI, Cowork, and Code.

The new Claude Science app arrives in beta today for macOS and Linux. Anthropic says it “runs analyses, searches databases, and traces every step from data wrangling to publication, so you can spend time on science.”

Claude Science is a public beta app, not a model. It uses the same Claude models your plan includes. What’s new is everything around them: the scientific tools, database connections, and compute integrations that let Claude run full analyses on your own infrastructure.

Anthropic explains why the new Claude Science app exists:

General AI assistants can discuss biology, but they can’t run a pipeline, navigate scientific databases, orchestrate cluster jobs, or keep track of what happened in a previous session. Claude Science manages compute environments per specialist, and saves full provenance on every result. The app ships with analysis specialists for genomics, single-cell, proteomics, structural biology, cheminformatics, and more.

It can connect natively to 60+ scientific databases and domain-specific open models. Claude Science uses the skills in NVIDIA’s BioNeMo Agent Toolkit to connect natively to the life sciences models and libraries in BioNeMo, including Evo 2, Boltz-2, and OpenFold3.

articles.title: Street Fighter 6 players furious about latest update as new character Yasmine is released
articles.subtitle: "Biggest winner of this SF6 patch is Tokon and Avatar" Related Street Fighter 6 just got its long-awaited Aug. 3 update, and the fan response has not been pretty.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
"Biggest winner of this SF6 patch is Tokon and Avatar"

Related

Street Fighter 6 just got its long-awaited Aug. 3 update, and the fan response has not been pretty. The short version is that the patch barely shakes up the game’s core systems, while making strange nerf and buff decisions for much of the roster.

For those who don’t play Street Fighter 6, Capcom has taken a very conservative approach to its balance updates, rarely changing the things outside new character releases. Once a year, the game receives a “major balance patch,” usually timed to avoid interfering with the Capcom Pro Tour competitive circuit. Because of these long delays between major alterations, there tends to be a great deal of anticipation around the yearly patch.

If there’s a main grievance with the latest update, it’s that it doesn’t alter Street Fighter 6 's increasingly divisive core systems. Specifically, there are no changes to Drive Rush and throw loops. Drive Rush lets every character close the distance by quickly charging forward. It has been criticized for making gameplay overly aggressive compared to previous Street Fighter games, as many characters have very quick Drive Rushes that are difficult to stop.

Throw loops are a technique that lets certain characters repeatedly throw their opponent in the corner. While throw loops aren’t inescapable, they put the defender in a disadvantageous position that can easily lead to a loss. It doesn't help that they are boring to execute and spectate. Many players have complained about both Drive Rush and throw loops for more than three years now, but Capcom has barely made any changes in response.

On top of the lack of significant system changes, many players are flabbergasted by the character buffs. Perhaps the most talked-about example is that Capcom made Ryu even better. Between his high damage and oppressive offense, he was already one of the best characters in the game, but he received improvements to one of his strongest attacks, Solar Plexus Strike.

The developers wrote in the patch notes that they thought this would “ make the move more balanced. ” Another dominant character, Sagat, received a mixture of nerfs and buffs that some think won’t negatively affect him. M. Bison, one of the most hated characters in the game, received buffs.

Meanwhile, other top-tier characters like Ed and Mai seem to have been severely nerfed. As for the rest of the cast, many characters received tiny updates that don’t seem likely to impact much. Not much seems to have changed at a high level, with the most significant character alterations seemingly being for the worse. Many are guessing the patch will drive more players to new fighting games like Avatar Legends and Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls.

If there’s a silver lining, it’s that the update coincided with the release of an all-new character, Yasmine, who players seem to be enjoying. She’s a fighter from the Philippines looking to find her brother, and fans have been taken by her stylish playstyle and wholesome relationship with her idol Manon.

While it will take time to see how Street Fighter 6 ’s latest update shakes out, the early reactions are not good. Yasmine’s release may be enough to bring some players back, but at least right now, her debut has been overshadowed by general disappointment with the game's stagnation.

articles.content:
Ever since Apple pulled out of Macworld New York back in 2023, August is traditionally a pretty slow month for Apple releases, but it’s a big one for the Apple rumor mill.

We don’t expect any new hardware this month with the looming iPhone/Apple Watch event coming in September. If you like your surprises spoiled, though, August is a good month for Apple rumors. Production will kick up for the new iPhones and Apple Watches, and sometimes other hardware that Apple plans to release in the fall. And with large-scale manufacturing comes leaks.

So August will probably be the month we get our best picture of the upcoming iPhones, Macs, and other devices Apple has planned for release this fall. Plus, the new operating systems are well into their public beta testing process—those will continue, but there probably won’t be any big surprises.

This will be Tim Cook’s last month as CEO, as John Ternus will take over the role on September 1. Oh, and Ted Lasso is back!

OS 27 beta testing continues

We don’t expect any new hardware in August (not with the big September iPhone event so close), but there will be plenty of software to check out if you participate in the beta program.

We’re currently at the fourth beta release for all the OS 27 updates: iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, visionOS. New releases go out to developers every two weeks or so, with the public beta testers getting the same builds a day or two later. So expect two more beta releases in August, potentially three.

At this point, most of the big features and changes in the OS 27 betas are already here, and Apple is just refining things, fixing bugs, and optimizing performance. We’ll be scouring the builds for potential hidden information about the upcoming products, too.

Despite receiving a price increase in June, the MacBook Air is currently experiencing a "major" shortage, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman.

"Retail store sources say Apple is struggling to keep the laptop in stock and that shipments of new units are more constrained than they can ever recall," he said.

In the U.S., the MacBook Air is facing a 2-6 week delivery estimate on Apple's online store, with configurations with higher amounts of RAM delayed the longest.

MacBook Air supply is constrained due to the ongoing memory chip shortage, resulting from companies building out data centers with powerful AI servers. In June, Apple raised prices on 14 products, including the MacBook Air. In the U.S., the laptop now starts at $1,299, up from $1,099. Despite this price increase, it appears that Apple is unable to keep up with demand right now.

articles.title: App report: Kicking my World Cup withdrawal
articles.subtitle: (Left to right): Annotate, Kickabout, and Undolly. For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days. But iOS remains a vibrant platform, too, and every now and again, we’ll look at some of the interesting apps being created for iPhones and iPads. This is one of those now and agains.

Want to see your app included in a future round-up? Get in touch at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of your app, and you just might make the cut.

Kickabout

The World Cup is just a memory now, but if you’re missing the daily infusion of soccer (or football, depending on what part of the globe you’re reading this from), Kickabout brings the action back to your iOS device in a very condensed form.

Kickabout will be immediately familiar to anyone who’s ever gathered around a foosball table in a rec room, with a look that will bring a smile to the face of Subbuteo tabletop football aficionados. You take charge of an 8-player team, with players only free to move about certain areas of the pitch. (No length-of-the-field Maradona-esque wonder golazos for your squad.

) You use your finger to drag your players around, swiping any which way to boot the ball toward the goal as you look to rack up the most goals in each 2-minute match.

Goals and shots off the post earn you points, which translates to tickets that you cash in to collect various national teams, from the U.S. all the way to newly minted world champion Spain. You can also buy gear, including stands for your virtual stadium. It’s a fun element that adds to Kickabout’s replayability as you try to assemble your own World Cup field.

Kickabout has both single-player and dual-player modes, though I found the latter to be a little cramped for my iPhone 17 screen. I imagine head-to-head matches are much more enjoyable on the iPad. Still, Kickabout offers plenty of fun even for single players, as you try to master the game’s different difficulty levels.

Kickabout is free to download, and a $3 in-app purchase gets rid of any ads.

Undolly

The Photos app has a built-in tool to weed out duplicate images, but if you find yourself taking a lot of photos, Undolly brings a whole suite of tools that promise to bring order to your iOS device’s photo library. Besides getting rid of duplicates, the mobile app also lists large videos taking up space in your library, rounds up any screenshots you may have stashed somewhere and keeps tabs on other potential space-takers like RAW, timelapse and animated images.

The value of Undolly will depend heavily on how you use your photo library. For instance, I take a lot of screenshots for articles that I don’t always remember to delete, and the app helped me track down some that were three to five years old. I also appreciate Undolly’s swipable comparisons of similar shots, so you can see for yourself whether the images differ enough to keep.

Undolly’s algorithm also rates images by their framing, quality and expressiveness of subject to better help you determine the shots that deserve a place in your library.

While it’s free to download initially, you will have to subscribe to Undolly to use its features, with a free three-day trial letting you get the lay of the land. After that, a monthly subscription costs $4, while annual and lifetime payments go for $15 and $40, respectively.

VWLSS

Nearly five years after Wordle first appeared, we’re still living in a golden age for daily word puzzles. Add VWLSS and its daily serving of mobile word play to the pile, though there are some unique iPhone elements that could help this free offering earn a place in your regular rotation of gameplay.

You have eight words to guess, each tied to a specific category and with all the vowels stripped out. It’s up to you to figure out the actual word, which you can do either by typing in the answer or using a handy speech feature. I prefer talking to typing, though I’m still sore that my guess of “Bob Barker” in the game show hosts category was misheard as “Bob Parker.” Revenge will be mine tomorrow, I guess.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation. articles.title: Pokopia’s Big Update Will Fix My Biggest Issue With The Game
articles.subtitle: Nintendo Switch 2 Pokémon Pokémon Pokopia Pokémon Pokopia ‘s first paid DLC, Bubbly Basin, is arriving in the game alongside a major free update on Wednesday.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Nintendo Switch 2 Pokémon Pokémon Pokopia

Pokémon Pokopia ‘s first paid DLC, Bubbly Basin, is arriving in the game alongside a major free update on Wednesday. While the big focus of that major update has been the new ability Ditto gets that lets them dive underwater, I’m almost even more excited about another feature we’ve just learned about: shared storage.

As reported by Famitsu and shared by Serebii, Pokopia ‘s free update will apparently include some sort of shared storage unit, which can hold up to 140 items and allows players to access stored items from anywhere a bin is placed. So if you put an item in a shared storage box in Withered Wasteland, you can put another shared storage box down in Bubbly Basin and get that item out.

Simple as this sounds, this is a game changer for Pokopia. A lack of shared storage was one of my biggest issues with this game. I understand it to an extent: Pokopia ‘s limited inventory essentially forces you to start over in each new region you visit, so you can’t easily haul resources from one place to another and fast-track yourself.

But after a certain point in the story, it becomes unwieldy and confusing to keep track of what you have in what bin in what region, and where in that region.

I’ve tried repeatedly to separate things out into decoration bins, resource bins, block bins, and so forth, but inevitably I get them all jumbled up in my brain and have to check every single bin everywhere before I finally find where I left that Wing Fossil head. ( The community is appropriately thrilled ).

Other cool info Serebii pulled from Famitsu includes more confirmed new Pokémon (Wiglett and Mareanie), frameless glass, a special item to generate electricity underwater, and the ability to use Rollout, Rototiller, Rock Smash, and Leafage underwater without issue.

The big Pokopia update drops on Wednesday, August 5. If you’ve bought the $35 expansion pass, you’ll also get access to the new region, Bubbly Basin. Everyone else will still get the Dive ability. Hopefully the shared storage box is part of the free update, too!

articles.title: Always choose the good soap
articles.subtitle: (Angelo D’Amico/Shutterstock) I’ve been thinking about soap again. Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation: We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’ve been thinking about soap again.

Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation:

We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we usually do. Because I’m me, I started thinking about Apple. Like Apple, the nice hotel’s brand promise is that it’s a nice hotel.

If the hotel didn’t clean its rooms well, didn’t provide soap that smelled nice, didn’t maintain the in-room refrigerator, didn’t clean the swimming pool, it would probably decrease its expenses and increase its profit margin. But over time, it would lose its niceness and become a lousy, overpriced hotel.

Earlier this month, John Gruber wrote about how he hopes incoming Apple CEO John Ternus can perform a bit of a reset on Apple’s advertising strategy. In recent months Apple has announced that it’s adding ads to Apple Maps, and ( as John has documented ) it’s allowed incredibly low-quality, scammy ads to infest Apple News.

While Apple can spin adding ads to Apple Maps as a revolutionary new way for businesses to be discovered, it’s telling that its initial announcement was hidden inside a press release about an entirely different product, and introduced as “Enhanced Discoverability in Apple Maps.

” Those choices show that this isn’t something Apple is actually proud of—and that the people in charge of communicating and explaining Apple’s decisions to the world are at odds with those who are making the decisions about expanding revenue.

Apple also recently expanded App Store ads, creating more clutter at the top of App Store search results. It similarly pitched this as an opportunity for developers—but of course, it’s really an opportunity for developers to take a portion of the money they make from the App Store after Apple’s cut and hand it right back to Apple so that their apps don’t become invisible. What a racket.

But Apple’s approach to grinding out additional revenue doesn’t stop with advertising. The recent release of Apple Creator Studio should’ve been a highlight, because it groups a bunch of useful creative apps in one place for a reasonable price. Instead, its launch was marred by the inclusion of Apple’s free productivity apps in the bundle, requiring users to download new versions and (at least initially) display aggressive subscription promotions in the Numbers, Pages, and Keynote interface.

To this day, you’re confronted with an ad for Creator Studio every time you create a new document in those apps, and their default toolbars contain buttons that won’t work unless you subscribe to the bundle.

As a result, Apple has essentially turned its free productivity suite—software that was designed to enhance the inherent value of Apple’s products—into a freemium package with upsell to a creative professional subscription bundle that’s irrelevant (and a terrible value! ) for most of its existing users.

There are many more examples. Using notifications to promote subscriptions and badging the Settings app to push AppleCare plans are among the ways Apple has chosen to intervene in the user experience to drive revenue.

I’m actually not opposed to the idea that Apple should communicate opportunities for its customers to get more out of their devices—but it should be careful not to cross the line into actively annoying those customers. If someone doesn’t want to see what you offer, you need to accept that and go away—not keep needling them. Apple often falls on the wrong side of that line.

Which brings me back to the hotel soap.

Apple’s most valuable asset is its brand. Not its real estate, not its intellectual property, not even any particular product. Even the mighty iPhone has no value if, over time, the traits that differentiate it from competitor products are erased. Apple’s brand has always stood for higher quality products—you pay more, but you get more. Apple has never wanted to be the low-price leader.

It didn’t put stickers on the first Intel Macs to get some marketing dollars from Intel. It doesn’t load up new Macs with loads of lousy bundled third-party software like so many PCs do.

Those are choices Apple has made that cost the company revenue, but they’ve got a bigger purpose. They reinforce the brand.

Opting not to add more revenue to the bottom line is a difficult choice for anyone working at a profit-driven corporation. I used to be in that position at my former employer, defending the overall product against a constant stream of advertising and biz-dev deal proposals that would add incremental revenue. Believe me, arguing to corporate executives that we should leave money on the table is a deeply uncomfortable role to take on—but it’s vital if you care about the bigger picture.

articles.title: How to keep your Mac awake, even when your MacBook lid is closed
articles.subtitle: macOS is designed to put your Mac to sleep when it is not being used. That is usually exactly what you want. Sleep saves power, protects battery life, and keeps a MacBook from running when it is closed and stuffed in a bag.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
macOS is designed to put your Mac to sleep when it is not being used. That is usually exactly what you want. Sleep saves power, protects battery life, and keeps a MacBook from running when it is closed and stuffed in a bag.

Sometimes tasks like downloads, backups, remote sessions, and AI coding need a temporary exception. Fortunately, there are some great Mac apps for giving you this control.

Limited solutions that are included with macOS

Apple gives you some control in System Settings.

On macOS, you can go to System Settings > Lock Screen to change when the display turns off, and on Mac laptops you can use System Settings > Battery > Options to prevent automatic sleeping on the power adapter when the display is off.

Apple also supports using a Mac laptop with the lid closed when it is connected to power and paired with an external display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad.

I generally prefer not to make those settings permanent. Most of the time, I want my Mac to sleep normally. What I want instead is a quick, intentional override that I can turn on for a specific job and turn off when I am done.

For that, there are three Mac utilities worth knowing.

KeepingYouAwake is the simple one-click toggle

KeepingYouAwake is the utility that has lived in my Mac menu bar the longest.

It is free, lightweight, and built around the same basic idea that made Caffeine popular years ago: click a menu bar icon, and your Mac stays awake. Click it again, and your Mac returns to its normal sleep behavior.

I started using KeepingYouAwake years ago when Macs moved to Retina displays. Caffeine, the classic coffee-cup utility, did not make that transition to high-resolution design.

KeepingYouAwake became the simple replacement. It honors the spirit of Caffeine with no dashboard or complex automation. It’s just a reliable on/off switch for the Mac’s default sleep behavior.

You can activate it indefinitely or for preset durations, and it can automatically disable itself when your MacBook battery drops below a set level. It supports Retina displays and Dark Mode, and under the hood it uses Apple’s built-in caffeinate command-line utility.

The important limitation: KeepingYouAwake is not the closed-lid solution. Its own documentation is clear that, because of macOS limitations and thermal considerations, it only prevents sleep on desktop Macs and portable Macs with the lid open.

That makes KeepingYouAwake ideal for the simple stuff: reading, presentations, screen recordings, long downloads, or any time you are still using the Mac and just do not want the screen or system to nod off. It is the utility I use as my everyday “do not sleep yet” toggle.

Amphetamine is the gold standard for closed-lid sessions

When I actually want to close my MacBook and keep a task running, Amphetamine is the app I open.

articles.title: Pokémon Center update could change everything for 30th anniversary pre-orders
articles.subtitle: Maybe actual collectors will be able to buy UPCs and ETBs now Related Trading card game fans have spent the last few weeks feeling anxious, as The Pokémon Center slowly doles out new waves of 30th anniversary pre-orders.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Maybe actual collectors will be able to buy UPCs and ETBs now

Related

Trading card game fans have spent the last few weeks feeling anxious, as The Pokémon Center slowly doles out new waves of 30th anniversary pre-orders. So far, the prevalence of bots programmed to make lightning-fast purchases while collectors wait for hours has made every drop a miserable affair. Much of the time, scalpers clean out the best products before most people can even load the page. But now, The Pokémon Company might finally be putting an end to that nightmare.

Retail-tracking Discord servers with access to The Pokémon Center's backend report that changes to the website's security measures are imminent. Previously, users hoping to buy cards had to complete a CAPTCHA before entering the queue. The system slowed down incoming traffic to the website, but it didn't really stop bots from gobbling up inventory.

Going forward, the system may work a little differently. A graphic shared on a number of major Pokémon Discord servers purports to show a new security check meant to thwart bots. One example prompts the user to grab a moving object that must be placed in the correct area. Based on the image, that security check appears to be Rotation Match with the other challenges titled 'Path Follow' and 'Target Align'.

While there are no examples of these security measures in the wild yet, it seems they will have some sort of dynamic element that cannot be easily automated.

Theoretically, this could mean that actual human beings will have an easier time getting into the queue to purchase Pokémon cards. But since the security measure has leaked before the system has gone live, proprietors of popular bot programs are already scheming potential workarounds.

For now, TCG collectors are rejoicing at the prospect of even a temporary setback for bot programs. The next drop is rumored to be the most expensive product in the 30th anniversary lineup, the Ultra Premium Collection. Vendors are already selling pre-orders for the $179.99 Eevelution-themed box at multiple times the manufacturer's suggested retail price. The general expectation was that, due to its high price tag and desirable promo cards, the UPC would be one of the most difficult items to source at MSRP.

Unless, of course, the new anti-bot measure goes live with the UPC pre-orders, which are reportedly already loaded into the Pokémon Center's backend. The Pokémon Center's alleged security updates would coincide with recent tweaks to Target and Walmart websites designed to curb bots and scalpers.

Whatever the case, Pokémon fans are bracing themselves for a potential new pre-order opportunity in the first week of August. Beyond the UPC, a number of other products, like the Ditto Premium Collection and the Figure Collection, have yet to go on sale. The first set of 30th anniversary products will be released on Sept. 16.
