articles.title: The better way to use Gemini on the Mac
articles.subtitle: Back in April, Google joined OpenAI and Anthropic in offering a dedicated Mac app for its AI chatbot software. Two months later, it’s clear that Gemini for Mac isn’t as good as it could be.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Back in April, Google joined OpenAI and Anthropic in offering a dedicated Mac app for its AI chatbot software. Two months later, it’s clear that Gemini for Mac isn’t as good as it could be.

Gemini for Mac isn’t a very good macOS app

Because I’m interested in AI technology and its progression over time, I’ve used Gemini on my Mac regularly since before the Mac app was rumored.

I’m also a Safari user. For that reason, my solution to using Gemini on the Mac has been Safari’s “Add to Dock” feature.

When Gemini first arrived on the Mac as a dedicated app, I still preferred my Safari “Add to Dock” instance. I just like that Command + N opens a new chat window, and I can have many open chat windows.

This way of multitasking is better for me than switching between conversation threads. I’m more likely to forget about a task in a chat thread if it’s not an open window on my Mac.

Missing features and app icon jail

I also have at least one chat thread that doesn’t actually work on Gemini’s Mac app. It works fine in the Safari “Add to Dock” version, though, since that’s just the website presented as an app.

Instead of letting me continue the chat, Gemini’s Mac app replaces the text entry box with a button to open the website. I’d rather just use my Safari web app version where it works fine.

The use of the word “yet” in the message is doing a lot of work at this point.

Another complaint is the icon. Gemini’s Mac app is in icon jail.

Icon jail is a dumb Apple behavior for app icons on macOS Tahoe that aren’t drawn in the exact shape and size that Apple forces.

While that’s an Apple-forced problem for Mac apps that predate Apple’s dumb rule, the Gemini Mac app arrived months after macOS Tahoe was released.

Then there’s the thing that prompted me to mention how I’m using Gemini on my Mac in the first place.

This week on Daring Fireball, John Gruber wrote about why he uninstalled the Gemini Mac app:

The thing that really turns me off about the Gemini Mac app is Google’s gall. The Gemini app installs a background helper named “GeminiAppLauncher” in your login items. It also installs “GoogleUpdater” as a process with the privilege to launch in the background whenever it wants. Gemini never asks for permission to install either of these, and, most arrogantly, if you, as an informed user, remove either of them, the Gemini app silently adds them back. There is no setting in Gemini to disable this.

This made me realize that I’ve literally kept the Gemini Mac app around just to check for app updates. While there are occasional updates, they haven’t fixed my two issues with the software yet.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Xbox’s Disc-To-Digital Plan Rolls Out This August According To Leaked Roadmap
articles.subtitle: According to a leaked roadmap and a report sent to publishers that’s been reviewed by The Verge, Xbox’s previously reported disc-to-digital program will roll out to the general public this month.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
According to a leaked roadmap and a report sent to publishers that’s been reviewed by The Verge, Xbox’s previously reported disc-to-digital program will roll out to the general public this month. The roadmap also indicated that a wider rollout of original Xbox games on PC would take place in October, while Xbox 360 games are set to arrive on current-gen consoles beginning next year and into 2028. On X, a Brazilian language account shared a graphic of the roadmap that you can check out here, or see below.

The disc-to-digital program is an attempt at future-proofing the potential forthcoming end of physical disc drives by granting users a transferable digital license for games they own on disc. If a user inserts an Xbox One or Series X game disc into a console, it automatically creates a digital license for the game that’s bound to the player’s account.

That license can be utilized across Xbox devices but should the disc be used by another party, say after the original owner has sold it at a GameStop, the license will transfer to its new owner and the original owner will lose access to the game.

In addition to disc-to-digital, Xbox has other plans for making its back catalog more widely available. Last month, Xbox released four of its original games on PC — Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy— and the roadmap suggests it’s bringing more to PC this fall. Xbox also included a note to publishers in the leaked document.

For both programs, Xbox manages all engineering, certification, and support efforts. You, the publisher, keeps full control over rights, pricing, and brand; your only lift is opting in and setting commercial terms. Both programs reactivate dormant SKUs, unlock new audiences on PC and handheld, and create ready-made re-release opportunities — no porting efforts required.

All of these developments seem to be a part of Asha Sharma’s great Xbox reset. And while these developments are heartening for those of us with a library of physical Xbox games (or those who just want to ensure Lost Odyssey remains accessible in the near and far future), there is a cynicism to it all.

When you’ve all but stopped up your new release schedule by cancelling projects, gutting your development teams, and spinning off the rest, the only way you’re gonna get new content in your pipeline is by filling it with old stuff.

articles.subtitle: SuperDuper has been an incredible tool for backing up your Mac for a long time, but like most apps that last 22 years, things change. Developer David Nanian has launched a new version that is ready for the next 22 years.

articles.content:
SuperDuper has been an incredible tool for backing up your Mac for a long time, but like most apps that last 22 years, things change. Developer David Nanian has launched a new version that is ready for the next 22 years. He writes:

Back in 2007, I designed what was intended to be SuperDuper v3. 0. It was a rewrite that greatly expanded its capabilities while retaining its essence. But, in those days, it just wasn’t possible for us to implement those grand plans.

The new UI was much more complex, the logic more elaborate, and the systems we had then didn’t support the things needed to make it a reality without a lot of complex coding we didn’t have time for. On top of that, macOS itself was a moving target (and still is! ): adding and deprecating features; completely changing the file system; locking down the OS; supporting not just one change in CPU, but three.

With a tool so tied to how the system operated at a low level, it was a lot of work just keeping up with what Apple was doing. So, I put the notebook with that design in it on a shelf. For nearly 20 years. Today, I’m happy to say that I’ve finally been able to carve out enough time to grab that “old” redesign, flesh it out further, modernize it, and make that dream a reality.

The new version of SuperDuper is a ground-up rewrite, a tip-to-tail reinvention of what SuperDuper looks like, how it works, what it can do, and where I can take it in the future.

articles.title: Unlock or recover your Mac using a special boot volume
articles.subtitle: Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid in Disk Utility, or reinstall Mac OS X or macOS. Over the years, Apple has multiplied those hidden locations and added more sophistication to what they offer.

These boot volumes are:

recoveryOS: The current name and form of the special volume described above, which boots into the Recovery Assistant “app. ” You can run Disk Utility (and First Aid), reinstall macOS, launch Safari to access Apple Support pages, modify startup security settings (rarely required these days), and access Terminal. With Terminal, you can reset your macOS password.

If your Mac can’t start up properly, it will try to launch the Recovery process within recoveryOS, which performs automatic repairs that Apple doesn’t document. If successful, you can then restart into macOS.

Fallback recoveryOS: If recoveryOS is damaged—and that can happen—you can press the power button twice, quickly, and then keep holding it the second time. This fallback recovery volume can’t change startup security, but it can help you diagnose what’s going on. This is the duct-tape belt that helps if your pants come unbuttoned (macOS won’t boot) and your suspenders break (regular recoveryOS fails).

Repair Assistant: From a powered-down state, press the power button until you hear the startup chime, then press and hold Command-D. (On an Intel Mac, hold the D key at startup. ) The Diagnostics app can run hardware tests that might help narrow down a problem before you bring in Apple Support, or they may ask you to boot into that mode and share the results of the tests they have you run.

Repair Assistant can fail, too, if its volume is damaged. You may then have to perform a special “ revive or restore ” operation, which requires another Mac. Or you may need a full reinstall using a bootable macOS installer.

macOS: macOS is a sort of hidden boot volume for the last several releases. You don’t boot from the system; instead, a read-only snapshot of the system is mounted, and then booted from. This is part of Apple making system resources immutable through cryptography and at startup.

Besides using recoveryOS for the above tasks, you might also need to use it to unlock your Mac after locking it in Find My and to reset your password using a FileVault Recovery Key. Here’s how.

Unlock your Mac

While it’s not a common scenario, it could happen to you: you accidentally leave your Mac somewhere, or it’s stolen. Thinking quickly, you launch Find My on another of your devices or go to iCloud. com/find and log in. You then tap or click a few buttons to lock your Mac. If the Mac is connected to the Internet, it restarts and locks immediately.

(Despite promising to display the message you entered when you locked it, macOS does not do so. ) If it’s not connected, it restarts the next time it has Internet access.

The account used to lock the Mac is the only one that can unlock it, and you must be in front of the Mac to perform that operation. Apple limits each Mac to having Find My enabled from a single account. Here are the steps:

When you see the macOS Recovery title, click the account profile below it. Enter the account’s password and click Continue.

If you entered it correctly, “Authentication succeeded” appears. Click Restart.

The Mac restarts and shows Activate Mac after it boots up. This time, all the active macOS accounts are shown. Click one, and then enter its password. Click Next.

You now can choose to either use your Apple Account or a macOS password to continue. If you opt for the Apple Account, enter the full address or phone number as shown. Then enter the account’s password. Otherwise, you can click to enter the Mac password, which Apple says is the last one used to unlock the Mac in a regular session before it was locked.

If you’re the only user on the Mac, that’s easy to figure out. (In testing with Golden Gate public beta 2, I wasn’t able to get the Mac password option to work, and I’ve had it fail in Tahoe, too. ) Sometimes neither works. Choose Restart from the Apple menu in that case and try again.

articles.title: Lil Finder Guy pet was the gateway to building my own Mac apps with Codex

articles.content:
At the start of May, OpenAI released a playful feature inside its Codex desktop app for creating a virtual pet.

This silly little addition solved my biggest challenge with Codex: what should I do with it? My first real task with Codex was putting together a virtual Lil Finder Guy for fun.

A month later, I’m using two Mac apps that Codex built at my direction. Toying around with Codex Pets was the gateway for me to better understand its capabilities.

OpenAI tools for making apps have improved a lot since last summer

Both Mac apps are just for my use and not intended for distribution, but that’s just a choice and not a Codex limitation. They’re genuinely usable and useful software applications that serve my needs.

One tool is called Flow, and it just helps me track activity and changes around the App Store. Another offers a better experience with using a social network on the Mac without certain constraints of Chrome, like minimum window width.

The experience taught me just how much these tools have changed since this time last year as well.

For example, I wanted to make my own Launchpad replacement when macOS Tahoe removed the feature from the Mac last June. (Launchpad wasn’t for everyone, but it was part of my muscle memory since OS X Lion. I’ve since moved on from missing it.)

Using ChatGPT to walk me through Xcode while copying and pasting blocks of code and screenshots of errors was a process void of much joy. Even as a proof-of-concept, I couldn’t get the app that I was making to resemble the behavior that I had in mind. Nuking the project felt good.

With Codex, I had a functioning app that solved my specific need in almost no time (and literally no Xcode). I was able to go from idea to minimum viable software almost immediately. The rest of my first month with Codex and making the app was spent adding features beyond my original need and getting more specific about how things should look and behave.

There are more tools that I want to make for myself next, and having Codex’s capabilities on the Mac has been a real boost.

(Next, I’ll be watching Apple’s WWDC announcements with a new eye for what additional capabilities become available. I’m also cautious about any changes that may break my newfound system for turning ideas into functioning tools.)

Computer Use in Codex is a major unlock

Part of what makes Codex good at this compared to my experience using ChatGPT a year ago is that the model and app are made for coding and generally just doing things for you.

ChatGPT will absorb most or all of this functionality as a feature within the main app, but the extent of this remains to be seen. For now, there’s one thing in particular about Codex that made all the difference in the world: Computer Use.

Codex is far from the only coding agent available on the Mac, and it’s not the only version with a computer use feature either. But Codex’s Computer Use feature is phenomenal. On the Mac, it works in the background without taking over your machine. For me, this has meant I’ve been able to use my Mac, uninterrupted, while this coding agent expertly follows my direction.

Codex’s Computer Use essentially unlocks the complete opposite experience from what ChatGPT provided in this department last summer. Instead of it providing me with guidance and not much perspective, I’ve been able to guide it and vastly expand my own perspective.

articles.title: Love and Deepspace Valko furor leads to game's worst month ever
articles.subtitle: The gacha game took a massive financial hit in the wake of the Valko controversy Related Since it was released in 2024, romance gacha game Love and Deepspace has been a massive hit for developer and publisher Papergames.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
The gacha game took a massive financial hit in the wake of the Valko controversy

Related

Since it was released in 2024, romance gacha game Love and Deepspace has been a massive hit for developer and publisher Papergames. It's been hugely popular with its devoted player base, who have been more than happy to shell out real-world money on its digital heartthrobs — until last month. New data shows Love and Deepspace 's revenue has hit an all-time low, and it's likely due to the biggest controversy the game has faced.

According to the latest reports from Sensor Data, Love and Deepspace pulled in just over $10 million in July. For reference, in June, the game's monthly revenue was closer to $40 million. Prior to this new low, revenue had never dropped below $30 million. The rapid and sudden drop coincides with the beginning of an ongoing Love and Deepspace controversy centered around the canceled character Valko.

In June, Papergames revealed new love interest, Valko. He was planned to debut as part of Version 6. 0 on July 9, becoming the sixth love interest in the game. The community was immediately divided on the character's reveal. A subset of fans, mostly in China, felt the introduction of a sixth love interest ignored the demand for meaningful updates to the game's existing love interests.

Anti-Valko sentiment grew so much that some disgruntled fans reportedly delivered cow dung to lockers at Papergames' offices. Eight days after his reveal, on June 30, Papergames announced the cancellation of Valko and any future love interests for Love and Deepspace.

This decision was immediately met with backlash from a different subset of the Love and Deepspace community, mostly international fans. It triggered a large debate about competing communities within the fanbase and the perception among international fans that Papergames prioritized Chinese players' preferences. "Bring back Valko" began trending across social media.

Multiple petitions were also started in hopes of convincing the developer to walk back the cancellation of Valko, at least on the game's international servers. During Anime Expo 2026, just days after Valko's cancellation, fans constructed a memorial for the character.

The Chinese government got involved a few days later. In an official post, the government took aim at Valko and the perception that his storyline glorified sexual assault and home intrusion. This was also a claim the Chinese player base made prior to the cancellation of Valko. The post went on to say that any game that deliberately blurs the lines of illegality would be removed.

While Papergames has made no further announcement on a possible future for Valko, it seems like he's gone for good. All this has prompted many disgruntled fans to abandon the game, and Papergames is now seeing the impact in Love and Deepspace 's revenue.

articles.title: Review: Xteink X3 is the little e-reader the world’s not quite ready for
articles.subtitle: An e-reader magneted to the back of a smartphone, just as the prophecy foretold. The market for small e-readers has been booming lately.
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The market for small e-readers has been booming lately. Earlier this year, Jason took a look at the Xteink X4, a pint-sized reading device that was about as light and small as they come. But those maniacs at Xteink weren’t done yet: they followed it up with the $79 X3, which is unbelievably even lighter and smaller.

I wouldn’t blame you for wondering if there’s such a thing as too small and light—at 3.84 inches by 2.51 inches (and just 0.2 inches thick) the X3 is still larger than, say, a credit card, but not by much. The screen itself measures just 3.7 inches, more than half an inch smaller than the X4’s 4.3 inch, but its 259 ppi resolution still makes it plenty easy to read on. 1 At that size it’s little imposition to take it with you wherever you go. Easy to lose? Maybe. Easy to love? Yes.

For one thing, this small size unlocks at least one capability that the X4 couldn’t fully deliver upon—the ability to stick to the back of your phone. Like the X4, the X3 has a MagSafe-compatible magnet in its rear case and it fits just about perfectly on the back of my iPhone 17 Pro, nestled below the camera plateau.

However, the magnet is not particularly strong, and it lacks the secondary stabilizing magnet that you see on official MagSafe accessories, meaning it wobbles around a bit. I wouldn’t call it a super secure connection, but it’s pretty good if you’re just slipping it in and out of a pocket. Just be aware that it probably will come loose.

Like the X4 before it, the X3 features a pair of rocker switches on the front for a total of four possible buttons. But they’ve opted to skip the X4’s side mounted rocker switch in favor of a single buttons on each side. There’s also an on/off switch at the top (plus a recessed button used for resetting the device). And with all of that, they somehow managed to continue to fit a microSD slot in the top. The bottom left corner also has a little set of holes for a lanyard or wrist strap.

The one casualty of the smaller X3, however, is the port. The X4 was big enough to accommodate a USB-C connector, but the X3’s thin profile makes that impossible. Instead, there’s a pogo-pin USB cable that connects to four magnetic contacts on the reader. Is this a step back? Strictly speaking, yes.

Using a proprietary connector is a bummer in the year 2026, especially because it means having to keep track of a single-use cable. That said, once you get the X3 up and running, the only real need for the connector is charging, and the battery on this thing lasts a very long time. (I’ve yet to run it down in several weeks of usage.

) Just remember to make a note of where you stow that cable for the point months down the road when you do need to charge it and find yourself wondering whatever happened to it.

As with the X4, the X3 lacks any sort of screen lighting, meaning that it’s strictly a “read in bright light” device. But don’t worry, because Xteink has already unveiled a new X4 Pro with the company’s first lit screen. 2

All in all, I found the X3 very comfortable to read on, whether attached to my iPhone or not. The side buttons work great as page-turners, and the screen is high-contrast and sharp enough to make text render very clearly. All in all, it’s a great reading experience—if you take into account one major caveat.

Soft where?

The elephant in the room for the Xteink X3 is the software. Xteink ships the X3 with its own built-in firmware which, by all accounts, has improved since the first version. But I can’t really tell you, because upon opening the box and powering up the device, the first thing I did was install Crosspoint, the open-source community-built firmware that has turned this device from a curiosity into a real contender. 3

Unlike a lot of other firmware replacements, Crosspoint is super easy to install; you can do it right from a web browser. While it’s not fully free of technological hurdles, I’d say that most people comfortable using an e-reader or updating their iPhones will be able to handle the process with few problems. And the benefits are manifold.

Crosspoint goes beyond simply turning this into a functional device and into one that is actually fun to use. It’s got a straightforward, easy to navigate interface that makes it simple to do everything from reading to loading books (accomplished via a web-based interface). For those who like to tweak their reading setup, there are plenty of configuration options, everything from screen orientation to hyphenation and, yes, custom fonts loaded via the SD card.

Even the onscreen keyboard that you need to use for various configuration tasks is pretty solid for what’s available—on par with navigating via an onscreen keyboard with a game controller, in my opinion. I wouldn’t want to have to type in my Wi-Fi password every time—and you don’t, because it saves it for you—but one time was fine.

There are also a bunch of other features that might appeal to those who want to take reading to the next level. For example, support for Open Publication Distribution System (OPDS) standard means that if you want to host your book library on your own server, you can point your reader at that and download any of the books you already own directly to your device. There’s also support for KOreader sync to help keep your place between supported devices. 4

Crosspoint has been so successful, in fact, that the team at Xteink has smartened up and started collaborating. (This after a brief moment when it looked like the company might try to firmware lock its devices.

) Now, not only do the “developer editions” sold directly by the company continue to allow you to install the custom firmware, the company has been working with the Crosspoint team to make sure new devices, like the X4 Pro, will already be supported when they arrive. While Xteink hasn’t quite adopted Crosspoint as the default OS, it’s not far off.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

articles.title: Is Apple ready to move at the speed of AI?
articles.subtitle: Macworld When Apple releases the OS 27 updates in a couple months, everyone’s iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch will get a real proper conversational AI installed. Siri AI, as Apple calls it, is more than just a basic phone voice assistant.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
When Apple releases the OS 27 updates in a couple months, everyone’s iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch will get a real proper conversational AI installed.

Siri AI, as Apple calls it, is more than just a basic phone voice assistant. It’s a standalone app with a full conversation history that can take complex prompts and deliver answers from a broad set of knowledge. You can upload documents to it and ask it to perform actions. In other words, it’s like ChatGPT, or Gemini, or Claude. Only it’s going to be pre-installed on hundreds of millions of devices.

Like it or not, the new Siri AI is going to be competing with, and judged by the standards of, those other popular AI tools. And all those competitors have set a pace and expectation for major new releases every few months rather than once a year. If Apple isn’t prepared for a Siri AI cadence that resembles other AI companies, it’s just going to appear hopelessly behind, right where it has been for the last two years.

To be clear, the new Siri AI is a massive improvement over old Siri in just about every way. It understands you better, it’s smarter, it gives you answers and context that the old Siri could never. Being able to pull context from Messages, Mail, Contacts, and web history results in delightful personalized answers that really make Siri start to feel like your assistant.

But it’s no ChatGPT, or Claude, or Gemini. Those other frontier models, despite their own problems, have access to far more information and a much deeper understanding of complex queries. They can take much bigger and more complex inputs and do much more interesting and detailed things with it. Once Siri becomes a full chatbot, it’s going to be compared against the chatbots people use today, and it’s going to come up wanting—except for its access to your on-device personal data, which is a major advantage.

In the short term, Siri AI’s shortcomings are not going to be a big problem. Users will be so overjoyed that “Siri doesn’t suck anymore” and impressed by some of the genuinely useful things it can do that they’ll overlook how much better other AI models are at so many things. But the honeymoon period won’t last, and it’s only a matter of time before users start looking at the latest from Google, OpenAI, or Anthropic and asking, “Why can’t Siri do this?”

Siri AI needs frequent major updates

Apple is accustomed to making significant improvements to core components only once a year, mostly aligned with the introduction of its new operating systems. For most things, that’s fine. For AI, that’s an absolutely glacial pace. In the last year alone, the major foundation AI models have released many big model updates:

Anthropic — Claude Opus 4.1, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Opus 5 along with other variants like Mythos, Fable, and Sonnet.

OpenAI — ChatGPT 5, GPT 5.1, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.3, GPT 5.4, GPT 5.5, and GPT 5.6.

Google — Gemini 3 Pro, 3 Deep Think, 3.1 Pro, 3.5 Flash, along with variants like Nano Banana Pro and Flash Lite.

In addition to these model updates, these products constantly add new capabilities. New image generation and editing. Video generation. New voice modes. New vision capabilities. Connections to other apps and services and the early stages of agentic (AI that can take actions on your behalf) capabilities. That’s not to mention the huge emphasis on developer-focused stuff like AI coding, interface and art generation, and frameworks to integrate into other products.

Apple’s biggest Siri AI model is based on the same technology foundation as Google’s Gemini, but with Apple’s own training data, weights, safeguards, etc. So it’s essentially Apple’s own foundation model, which it calls Apple Foundation Model (AFM) 3. After the release of the OS 27 updates in September, Apple will expand the availability of Siri AI to new languages and regions in the months that follow. That’s good, but it is far from enough.

For both the models that run on our iPhones and Macs (AFM 3 Core) and on cloud servers (AFM 3 Cloud), Apple needs to release multiple significant updates every year. We can imagine a release cadence: AFM 3.1 in December, AFM 3.2 in March, and AFM 3.5 in May, etc. All leading up to AFM 4 with the OS 28 updates.

This sort of update schedule, with significant and obvious improvements to the quality of Siri AI throughout the year, is table stakes in the AI race but utterly foreign to the way Apple usually operates. To fail to take up a release schedule like this is to invite the same unfavorable comparisons Apple has labored under for the last two years: that all the other AI products just put Siri to shame.

Can Apple do it?

Apple isn’t used to operating this way. It’s used to pushing out a big OS update in the fall, then following it up with a few tweaks and additional features in point releases while it spreads its latest features to all the languages and regions it supports.

A development schedule that releases a major update to a core technology several times a year would be a big change for Apple, but this might just be the time to make it.
